title: How I Give Technical Feedback to an Engineer Who's More Technical Than Me
author: Wojciszko, Karol
summary: Written by an engineering manager who no longer writes production code, this piece addresses a specific credibility problem: how to give meaningful technical feedback to engineers who are more technically skilled than you are, without faking expertise you don't have. The author names the common failure mode directly — skimming a few merge requests before a 1:1 and presenting surface-level observations as if you'd been closely tracking someone's work — and explains why it backfires: one exposed bluff (getting caught not understanding an answer to a real technical question) discounts every future piece of feedback from that manager. His alternative is a repeatable, honest system built on two legs: reading objective signal from tools like GitLab and Jira (merge rate, review time, task shape, error ownership, review footprint) to spot patterns without judging code quality directly, and explicitly sourcing qualitative, code-level feedback from a tech lead or senior peer closer to the work, always transparently attributed rather than presented as the manager's own insight. The underlying argument is that credibility comes not from closing the technical gap through pretense, but from being honest about where your own knowledge ends and building a system that reliably fills the rest.
points: Names the exact failure mode precisely: skimming a few merge requests the night before a 1:1 and presenting it as ongoing close tracking — which collapses the moment a real technical question exposes the bluff.
Once a manager is caught faking technical depth once, every subsequent piece of their feedback gets discounted by the team.
Proposes reading objective signals instead — merge rate, review time, MR size, error/Sentry ownership, review footprint — as a repeatable, non-bluffable feedback foundation.
For genuinely specific, code-level feedback, sources it transparently from a tech lead or senior peer and says exactly where it came from rather than presenting it as his own.
quotes: Pretending you reviewed the code is worse than admitting you didn't. And once you get caught faking depth once, every future piece of feedback from you gets discounted. That's the real cost.

The instinct is to compensate by forcing some kind of technical analysis anyway, hunting for something clever to say about the code itself. The moment you improvise an opinion on something you can't defend, you're not giving feedback anymore, you're gambling with your credibility.

GitLab and Jira generate more signal about how someone actually works than most managers ever look at. Merge rate, review time, MR size, comments given and received, lines changed, deployment activity. None of it requires reading a single diff.
Before every feedback session, I collect input from whoever is closest to the work. When I bring that feedback into the room, I say exactly where it came from. I don't present it as mine.

What actually works is being honest about where your own view ends, and building a system that fills in the rest instead of hiding it. Metrics tell you the shape of the work. The people closer to the code tell you the substance.
